endorsements.quote: For this reason, we recommend anyone performing any analysis of medical images to employ multiple statistical rates, and not only one.
Splitting the dataset into a training set and a test set, by making sure that no data element is shared between the two, is a key pillar of any supervised machine learning analysis [ 5 ].

unlisted_practices: Ensure sufficient computational resources (storage, RAM, HPC or GPUs) before starting a medical image analysis project.
Conduct power analysis and sample size calculations before conducting experiments.
Handle class imbalance using techniques such as data weighting, oversampling, undersampling, and data augmentation.
Apply denoising to medical images before analysis rather than analyzing raw data.
Apply image harmonization to minimize scanner and site variations when combining multi-institution datasets.
Use open source programming languages and software, and avoid proprietary software.
Release analysis software code publicly on repositories to enhance reproducibility.
Reduce overfitting through feature selection and dimensionality reduction, keeping the number of features below 10% of the sample size.
Repeat dataset splits many times (at least 100) and check that results hold on both subsets.
Seek an external validation cohort dataset from public repositories and replicate the analysis on it.
Have a radiologist or medical doctor review medical image analysis results before publication.
Investigate model interpretability using explainable AI frameworks, with domain expert application-grounded evaluation.
Release datasets publicly following FAIR principles after obtaining ethical committee and patient authorizations.
Publish in open access journals when possible.

screen.reason: The paper provides guidance and best practice tips for computational and machine learning analysis of medical images to improve methodological quality and reproducibility.
